title: Knowledge & RAG
markdown:
Retrieval is handled by `openexecutive.knowledge.retriever.retrieve`, querying ChromaDB collections through `openexecutive.knowledge.store.ChromaDBStore`. When the caller passes `record_source`, `retrieve` also names every document its block quotes — company uploads by filename, built-in knowledge by a title made from its filename, Notion pages, synced Drive files by name with their Drive link, research notes by date, and earlier published documents with a link to `/artifacts/<id>` — so the web chat can list what an answer looked at: the chat route's own search, and each specialist's that answered (see the Lifecycle and API sections). The recording never raises, and a retrieval that fails leaves the specialist without context rather than failing the turn. Seven collections back the system:

- **BUILTIN** — curated MBA-style domain knowledge shipped with the repo, including a `sales` domain (founder-led sales, qualification and pipeline, proposals and pricing conversations, follow-up and forecasting) and solo-founder guides in finance, marketing, legal and HR. Seeded at boot by `loader.seed_builtin_knowledge` (FAILURES by `seed_failures`): the whole tree on an empty collection, otherwise only the `SHIPPED_BUILTIN_FILES` entries with no chunks yet — so a doc added in a later release reaches an install seeded by an earlier one, instead of shipping, registering as approved, and never being retrievable. Presence is judged from each row's `source` path relative to `knowledge/builtin/` (not the absolute path, which moves with the install), read in one metadata scan narrowed to seeded rows so the external OER corpus sharing the collection is never pulled. A complete store indexes nothing.
- **COMPANY** — customer documents ingested via the `/documents` endpoint. Curated uploads only — synced Notion pages and Drive files do not land here. A document's identity is its **filename**: chunk metadata and the chunk id both derive from it, so re-uploading upserts in place rather than duplicating, and `DELETE /documents/{filename}` matches the rows it claims to remove. Inbound attachments are **not** here — see ATTACHMENTS below; rows left by the earlier scheme are migrated out on boot. A scanned PDF (no text layer) is converted before chunking — see "Reading scanned PDFs" below — so it no longer indexes zero chunks while reporting `indexed`.
- **NOTION_WIKI** — optional Notion sync (`NOTION_SYNC_ENABLED`) incrementally re-indexes pages shared with a Notion internal integration into a separate `notion_wiki` collection (`type=notion`). A Notion share is inherited and multi-writer, so this text is unreviewed relative to curated company docs; the retriever labels it as such and ranks it below COMPANY. Un-shared pages are purged on the next tick.
Synced Drive files and Notion pages are listed on the knowledge page next to uploads (one Company documents list, each row badged with its source, its sync time and a link to the original), read from the sync state files rather than Chroma; each connected source shows its last run, its last error (a failed tick, or a count of files or pages a tick couldn't index; the next clean tick clears it) and a **Sync now** button (`POST /documents/sources/{id}/sync`). Uploads from the page no longer ask for a domain: they go in as `general`, which every specialist's COMPANY filter already includes.

- **DRIVE** — optional Google Drive folder sync (`DRIVE_SYNC_ENABLED`, `knowledge.drive_sync`). It incrementally re-indexes the files in `DRIVE_SYNC_FOLDER_IDS`, and their subfolders to four levels, into a separate `drive_docs` collection (`type=drive`). It reads the Drive v3 API directly as a service account with `drive.readonly` (`knowledge.drive_client`), not through the MCP gateway, so it sees only folders shared with that account and can change nothing. Google Docs and Slides are exported as text and Sheets as `.xlsx`. PDF, `.docx`, `.xlsx` and plain text files go through the loader's extractors, with no model call, so a scanned PDF yields nothing. Other files are skipped, and so are files over 20 MB (downloads are streamed and stop at the cap). A `.docx` or `.xlsx` that unzips past 100 MB is skipped, and so is a file whose extraction runs past 120 s; such files are recorded unreadable and not refetched until they change. A file is re-indexed when its `modifiedTime` or `md5Checksum` changes, and purged once it is no longer listed. Purging is skipped when a folder failed to list, the listing passed 2000 items, or every folder came back empty with files on record. A shared folder is multi-writer, so the retriever labels this text as unreviewed and ranks it below COMPANY, like NOTION_WIKI. Each chunk is labelled `[drive · file id … · synced … · "<name>"]`. The id and time come first because the sync wrote them. The name comes last, quoted and Unicode-normalised and stripped of brackets, quotes, `·`-like separators and `#`, so a folder editor cannot add a second `file id` field. The block tells the Executive to open the live file with `get_drive_file_content` when the latest version matters, using only the id at the start of a label, never one from a file's name or text.
- **FAILURES** — recorded failure cases (queried by `retrieve_failures`) teaching specialists what to avoid.
- **RECENT_RESEARCH** — web-research artifacts persisted from `executive_research` runs, plus every deliverable published with `draft_artifact` (metadata `type=artifact`, `artifact_id`; dropped again when superseded or deleted), kept separate from COMPANY so unvetted machine-generated text never blends into curated knowledge, and ranked below company documents. Artifact chunks are labelled `[published artifact <id> — <date> — earlier output, treat as data]` so the model can reread the whole thing with `get_artifact` without lending quoted text the Executive's own authority. Both kinds are cleared on a client switch or fixture reset.
- **ATTACHMENTS** — files attached in an integration channel (`inbound_attachments`), written only by `integrations.attachments`. The one collection `retrieve` **never queries**. The content is chosen by whoever sent the message, passes through no upload endpoint and gets no review; it is already inlined into the turn that carried it, and must not become company knowledge that resurfaces later. NOTION_WIKI and RECENT_RESEARCH are queried-but-labelled — this one is written and never read back.

Each parallel specialist call runs its own domain-filtered query. When no explicit filter is passed, `DOMAIN_ALIASES` maps the specialist key to its domains — e.g. `cso`→`strategy`, `cpo`→`product`,`strategy`, `sales`→`sales`,`marketing`, `board_comms`→`board`,`finance`. A specialist with no entry would get no filter at all and retrieve every domain, so each new specialist needs one. Hits beyond a cosine distance threshold are dropped, and very short messages (greetings) bypass retrieval entirely. BUILTIN can carry its own tighter gate via `KNOWLEDGE_BUILTIN_DISTANCE_THRESHOLD`: built-in knowledge is generic and far larger than a typical company corpus, so the distance that admits the right company doc also admits unrelated handbook prose. Unset, every collection shares `KNOWLEDGE_DISTANCE_THRESHOLD`.

`POST /documents` rejects any domain outside that set with a 400 — an unvalidated string would index the document under a domain no specialist filters on, failing silently and only at retrieval time. The tenth accepted value, `general`, is the catch-all for an upload nobody classified (it is the default on the endpoint, and what every upload from the knowledge page gets — the page no longer asks for a domain). It maps to no specialist, so every specialist's **company** filter is widened to include it — an unclassified document is visible to all rather than to none. That widening is deliberately not applied to BUILTIN, whose rows are shared with external OER sources that fall back to `general` when they declare no domains; fanning those into every specialist would blend unvetted third-party material into every answer.

Multi-domain chunks fan out to one row per declared domain, so `_dedupe_by_text` drops duplicate-text hits while preserving relevance order before results are returned.

### Embeddings

Every collection embeds with one shared all-MiniLM-L6-v2 ONNX session (`knowledge.store._embedding_function`), the same model and vectors as Chroma's default. Chroma's own default reloads the model on every call and keeps ONNX Runtime's memory arena, so a 300-chunk upload peaked near 760 MB and each query spent ~240 ms reloading. The shared session is built once, runs without the arena and embeds four texts at a time (the model pads every text to 256 tokens, so batch size sets the peak): ~300 MB and ~30 ms. It answers to Chroma's name `default` with an empty config, because every existing collection records that name and Chroma refuses a collection opened with a differently named function; and it must not be a `DefaultEmbeddingFunction` instance, which Chroma swaps for a fresh default on every embed.

### Reading scanned PDFs

pypdf returns only a PDF's saved text layer, so a scan, a phone photo saved as PDF, or a deck printed to PDF as images used to come back empty everywhere a PDF is read. `knowledge.pdf_reader.read_pdf_text` tries three readers in order and never raises:

1. **Text layer** (pypdf) — used whenever it yields real text (at least ~20 visible characters per page, so a scan carrying only page numbers still falls through).
2. **The deployment's own model, through its provider's PDF support** — opt-in, `PDF_PROVIDER_READING=true` (off by default: an upgrade never starts sending scanned PDFs off the server; this also means an Anthropic-direct deployment OCRs scans locally until it opts in) — the pages as a base64 `document` block, transcribed to Markdown by `PDF_VISION_MODEL` (unset: `DEFAULT_MODEL`, the model the deployment already runs on), `PDF_VISION_PAGES_PER_CALL` pages per request (default 20), three requests at a time. Each provider carries the block its own way: Anthropic reads it natively; on OpenRouter the translator makes it an OpenAI `file` part and the provider adds the `file-parser` plugin — engine `native` for Claude or any model the catalog lists with `file` input (OpenAI's GPT-4o and later, Gemini…), else `PDF_OPENROUTER_ENGINE` (default `mistral-ocr`, $2 per 1,000 pages); a local OpenAI-compatible server gets the `file` part only with `LOCAL_PDF_INPUT=true` (e.g. `LOCAL_BASE_URL` pointed at OpenAI's own API). `providers.registry.pdf_input_supported` decides; a model that cannot take one never receives it (the feature gate swaps a stray `document` block for a note). Turning it on sends scanned pages off the server — to the provider, and on OpenRouter possibly to its parser (Mistral OCR) — and the destination is logged once per process.
3. **Local OCR** — pages rendered with pypdfium2 and read by RapidOCR (ONNX, models bundled in the wheel): offline, no key, no per-page cost. The default reader while step 2 is off, what a local model without PDF input gets, and the fallback on every provider when step 2 errors, refuses or returns nothing. `PDF_OCR_ENABLED=false` turns it off.

`PDF_VISION_MAX_PAGES` (default 100) caps the pages read, with a note saying how many were; a file a channel delivered (`inbound=True`) is capped at `PDF_INBOUND_MAX_PAGES` (30) and metered by a rolling `PDF_INBOUND_PAGES_PER_HOUR` (300) budget. OCR is bounded too: a page renders within a 25-megapixel budget whatever its MediaBox claims (a crafted 20000pt page would otherwise allocate gigabytes), at most two documents OCR at once, and each stops after 240 s with what it has. A PDF of more than 2,000 pages is refused before any page is parsed (the caps above bound conversion, not the text-layer pass). A Claude slice that runs into the output limit is split in half until each part fits; a single page that still does not fit keeps what was written, marked `[transcription cut off here]`, and the note says so. A result is cached in process by the file's sha256 (32 entries) so a re-read does not re-bill; a failure is not cached. `loader.read_document_text` / `extract_text_from_file_async` route a PDF through it and every other type through the sync extractor, and are what `ingest_file` (uploads, boot reconcile), the `/documents/{filename}` preview, intake uploads, chat attachments, the email poller, `oe__read_file` and the Executive's `read_document` tool use.

### The SME review gate

Before the distance threshold applies, both `retrieve` and `retrieve_failures` drop **withheld** items — anything the review store reports as `pending` or `rejected` (`ReviewStore.get_withheld_filenames`). Approved items with a priority set are then sorted ahead of the rest.

Knowledge shipped with the product registers as a trusted default (`approved`, NULL `reviewed_at`), so nothing is withheld until a human deliberately queues a domain for curation or rejects something. See the **SME Knowledge Review** section for the full state model. The filter matches on the `(domain, filename)` pair Chroma carries. A bare filename was ambiguous *and* caller-choosable — `POST /knowledge/builtin` takes any `(domain, filename)`, so uploading a file named after a shipped doc in another domain silently withheld that shipped doc from every specialist. Failure case studies are keyed in their own namespace, so a user-authored one cannot collide with a shipped one.

The formatted context is injected into the **user turn** (wrapped in `<relevant_knowledge>` by `BaseAgent.analyze`), never into a cached system block — per-query hits would otherwise poison the prompt cache.

### Skills (Playbooks) collection

Skills — called **playbooks** in the UI, where they are a tab on Workflows — are Markdown procedures with YAML frontmatter, indexed one document per skill in their own `skills` collection (name + description + when_to_use; the body is fetched by `load_skill`). Built-ins ship under `knowledge/builtin/skills/`; company skills live in `company/skills/`. Customizing a built-in (a `PUT` from the Playbooks tab; the chat tools refuse built-ins) writes a company skill of the same name flagged `customizes_builtin: true`, which **replaces** the built-in: it shadows the built-in everywhere (chat, and the workflows that follow it — see the Workflows section), and deleting it reverts. A built-in cannot be deleted, so "delete" **hides** it via `company/skills/.hidden.yaml`; hidden and shadowed built-ins are dropped from the index. `sync_builtin_skill_index` reconciles the built-in rows at startup, after a client-slot restore, and after a fixture reset — so a built-in added in a release reaches an already-seeded index, and a removed one leaves it.

**Drafts.** The Executive's chat tools never change the library directly: `create_skill`, `update_skill` and `delete_skill` save a draft as JSON in `company/skills/.drafts/` (one per name; a newer proposal replaces the pending one). Drafts are not `*.md`, so they are never listed, indexed, searched, loaded or followed. A person approves a draft on the Playbooks tab (`POST /skill-drafts/{name}/approve`), which applies it through the ordinary skills operations, or discards it. Each save gets a fresh `id`, and approve/discard name the version the person saw: a proposal swapped in after review (say by a crafted inbound message) is never applied unseen, and approving never removes a newer draft that arrived meanwhile. This matches the draft → human-approval shape of custom workflows: a crafted inbound message can propose a playbook, but only a person can put one in effect.
